  1780  
  1781      \119\ For a full discussion on Transition Period and Effective 
  1782  Date, see section V.C above.
  1783  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1784  
  1785      Throughout the INA, Congress has drawn clear distinctions between 
  1786  different classes of aliens and the benefits to which they are 
  1787  entitled.\120 \The F-1 visa classification is for nonimmigrants who 
  1788  intend to come to the United States ``solely for the purpose of 
  1789  pursuing . . . a course of study'' and not an ancillary purpose, such 
  1790  as seeking employment.\121\ Additionally, the F-1 nonimmigrant 
  1791  classification is for aliens who have no intention of abandoning their 
  1792  foreign residence.\122\ A number of factors play a role in an F-1 
  1793  nonimmigrant student selecting an institution and course of study, 
  1794  including, but not limited to: geographic location, school rankings and 
  1795  prestige, program availability, campus culture, housing, sporting 
  1796  programs, and tuition costs. While DHS considered that the opportunity 
  1797  an institution provides for OPT may be one of many factors, it is 
  1798  speculative to assume that the ability to participate in OPT, which 
  1799  requires authorization by a SEVP-certified educational institution and 
  1800  the U.S. Government and is by law temporary in nature, is the sole 
  1801  reason a student decided to enter the United States on a F-1 
  1802  classification. In fact, only about 20 percent of F-1 nonimmigrants 
  1803  participated in OPT in 2024 out of the 1.4 million F-1 nonimmigrants in 
  1804  the higher education system, which demonstrates that the vast majority 
  1805  of F-1 nonimmigrants choose to study in the United States for reasons 
  1806  other than to pursue work through OPT.\123\ Regardless of whether F-1 
  1807  nonimmigrants participate in OPT, which is by definition not required 
  1808  to obtain their degree, they realize enormous benefits in studying at 
  1809  the prestigious institutions America offers and obtaining degrees from 
  1810  these institutions. Moreover, F-1 nonimmigrants may pursue appropriate

  1812  such as through the H-1B visa following graduation or on-campus or off-
  1813  campus employment during the program of study. Accordingly, DHS

[2026-14439: lines 16292-16541 of 19533, FR page 45105]
 16292  example, an F-1 student may enter their program anticipating it will 
 16293  take 4 years to complete, but they may then complete that program in 3 
 16294  years. Or an F-1 student may enter their program anticipating it will 
 16295  take 4 years to complete, but they may stop their studies completely 
 16296  after one semester. When an F-1 student ends their study or training 
 16297  early, that student, and any eligible dependents, must, within 30 days 
 16298  from the new end date, depart the United States or otherwise seek to 
 16299  maintain lawful status. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v).
 16300      Since an F-1 student now has 30 days, rather than the previously 
 16301  allotted 60 days, to depart the country or to otherwise maintain status 
 16302  after their completion of their program or program end date, it follows 
 16303  that they need to file a Form I-765 or successor form for post-
 16304  completion OPT within 30 days, rather than the previously allotted 60 
 16305  days, after their program end date. See new 8 CFR 
 16306  214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2). This has been retained in the final rule.
 16307      It similarly follows that a student may not request a start date of 
 16308  OPT employment which is more than 30 days (rather than 60 days) after 
 16309  the student's program end date. DHS overlooked this update to 8 CFR 
 16310  214.2(f)(11)(i)(D) in the NPRM but has made the change in the final 
 16311  rule. As explained in the response to comments above, DHS recognizes 
 16312  failing to make this update may cause confusion. This technical change 
 16313  aligns with the 30-day period that was proposed in the NPRM under 8 CFR 
 16314  214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2) and with the 30-day period of preparation for 
 16315  departure under 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v).
 16316      In the NPRM, DHS also proposed retaining the current regulatory 
 16317  language that allows a 15-day period for departure from the United 
 16318  States if an alien is authorized by the DSO to withdraw from classes, 
 16319  but no additional time for departure if the alien fails to maintain a 
 16320  full course of study without the approval of the DSO or otherwise fails 
 16321  to maintain status. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v). Because DSOs 
 16322  generally authorize withdrawal based on compelling academic or medical 
 16323  circumstances when a student proactively requests permission, DHS 
 16324  believes retaining the 15-day period is appropriate and has retained 
 16325  this provision in the final rule. However, aliens who fail to maintain 
 16326  their full course of study, are denied EOS, or
 16327  
 16328  [[Page 45106]]
 16329  
 16330  otherwise violate their status are required to immediately depart the 
 16331  United States, as is consistent with other nonimmigrant 
 16332  classifications. DHS considered allowing a short ``grace period'' for 
 16333  departure after an EOS denial but concluded there was not a compelling 
 16334  reason to treat F nonimmigrants who have received a denial more 
 16335  favorably than other nonimmigrant classifications. As in other 
 16336  nonimmigrant classifications, failure to immediately depart under these 
 16337  circumstances may result in accrual of unlawful presence and subject 
 16338  the individual to removal.
 16339  4. Automatic Extension of Authorized Period of Stay and Employment
 16340  a. Authorized Period of Stay and Employment Authorization Under 8 CFR 
 16341  214.2(f)(5)(viii)
 16342      Each year, a number of U.S. employers seek to employ F-1 students 
 16343  and file a Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, with USCIS, 
 16344  along with a change of status request, to obtain classification of the 
 16345  F-1 student as an H-1B nonimmigrant worker. The H-1B nonimmigrant visa 
 16346  program allows U.S. employers to temporarily employ foreign workers in 
 16347  specialty occupations, defined by statute as occupations that require 
 16348  the theoretical and practical application of a body of highly 
 16349  specialized knowledge and a bachelor's or higher degree in the specific 
 16350  specialty, or its equivalent. See INA sections 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) and 
 16351  214(i); 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) and 1184(i). The H-1B 
 16352  classification, however, is subject to annual numerical allocations, 
 16353  commonly referred to as a ``cap.'' See INA sections 214(g)(1)(A) and 
 16354  (g)(5)(C); 8 U.S.C. 1184(g)(1)(A) and (g)(5)(C).\323\ For purposes of 
 16355  the H-1B numerical allocations, each fiscal year begins on October 1. 
 16356  Petitioners may not file H-1B petitions more than 6 months before the 
 16357  date of actual need for the employee.\324\ Thus, the earliest date an 
 16358  H-1B cap-subject petition may be filed for an allocation for a given 
 16359  fiscal year is April 1, 6 months prior to the start of the applicable 
 16360  fiscal year for which initial H-1B classification is sought.
 16361  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16362  
 16363      \323\ Under INA 214(g)(1)(A), 8 U.S.C. 1184(g)(1)(A), 65,000 
 16364  aliens may be issued H-1B visas or otherwise provided H-1B 
 16365  nonimmigrant status in a fiscal year. This limitation does not apply 
 16366  to aliens who have earned a master's or higher degree from a U.S. 
 16367  institution of higher education, as defined in 20 U.S.C. 1001(a), 
 16368  until the number of aliens who are exempted from such numerical 
 16369  limitation during such year exceeds 20,000. INA 214(g)(5)(C), 8 
 16370  U.S.C. 1184(g)(5)(C).
 16371      \324\ See 8 CFR 214.2(h)(2)(i)(I).
 16372  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16373  
 16374      Many F-1 students complete a program of study or post-completion 
 16375  OPT in mid-spring or early summer. Per existing regulations, after 
 16376  completing their program or post-completion OPT, F-1 students have 60 
 16377  days (which DHS is proposing to change to 30 days) to take the steps 
 16378  necessary to maintain legal status or depart the United States. See new 
 16379  8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v). However, because the change to H-1B status cannot 
 16380  occur until October 1, an F-1 student whose program or post-completion 
 16381  OPT expires in mid-spring has two or more months following the 60-day 
 16382  period before the authorized period of H-1B status can commence. To 
 16383  address this situation, commonly known as the ``cap-gap,'' DHS 
 16384  established regulations that automatically extended F-1 D/S and, if 
 16385  applicable, post-completion OPT employment authorization for certain F-
 16386  1 nonimmigrants until April 1 of the fiscal year for which the H-1B 
 16387  status is being requested or until the validity start date of the 
 16388  approved petition, whichever is earlier. See redesignated 8 CFR 
 16389  214.2(f)(5)(vii). The extension of F-1 D/S and OPT employment 
 16390  authorization is commonly known as the ``cap-gap extension.'' This rule 
 16391  does not change the ``cap-gap extension'' provisions; it simply removes 
 16392  the reference to D/S and makes clear that an automatic extension will 
 16393  be granted to those with a fixed period of stay.
 16394  b. F-1 Status and Authorized Employment While EOS and/or Employment 
 16395  Authorization Applications Are Pending
 16396      DHS struck ``duration of status'' from redesignated 8 CFR 
 16397  214.2(f)(5)(vii) in the proposed rule and clarified that an alien with 
 16398  F-1 status whose admission period as indicated on his or her I-94 has 
 16399  expired, but who has timely filed an EOS application, will be 
 16400  authorized to continue pursuing a full course of study after the end 
 16401  date of his or her admission until USCIS adjudicates the EOS 
 16402  application. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii). This change allows for 
 16403  ongoing authorization to continue studies as long as the student has 
 16404  timely filed his or her EOS and will not penalize students if USCIS is 
 16405  unable to adjudicate an EOS application before a student's new term or 
 16406  course of study is underway. In such cases, students will be able to 
 16407  continue pursuing their full course of study.\325\ This change is 
 16408  retained in the final rule.
 16409  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16410  
 16411      \325\ However, if the extension of stay application is received 
 16412  during the 30-day period under new paragraph 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v), 
 16413  the F-1 student is authorized to continue a full course of study but 
 16414  may not continue or begin engaging in practical training or other 
 16415  employment. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B).
 16416  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16417  
 16418      DHS did clarify the title of new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii) in the 
 16419  final rule, since the automatic extension is for the authorized period 
 16420  of stay while the EOS is adjudicated, rather than an automatic EOS. The 
 16421  title changed from ``Automatic Extension of F stay and employment 
 16422  authorization. . .'' to ``Automatic extension of the authorized period 
 16423  of stay and employment authorization. . .''
 16424      The shift to a fixed date of admission has implications for various 
 16425  types of employment authorization. Prior to the effective date of this 
 16426  final rule, DSOs could authorize certain types of employment 
 16427  authorization, including on-campus employment and CPT,\326\ and 
 16428  students generally did not need to be concerned about a specific 
 16429  expiration date for their student status, and thus their employment 
 16430  authorization, because they were admitted for D/S. This rule changes 
 16431  that framework with different implications for various types of 
 16432  employment authorization.
 16433  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16434  
 16435      \326\ See 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)-(12), 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv).
 16436  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16437  
 16438      For on-campus employment where no EAD is needed, DHS is allowing 
 16439  aliens in F-1 status to continue to be authorized for on-campus 
 16440  employment while their EOS applications with USCIS are pending, not to 
 16441  exceed a period of 240 days.\327\ See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii). If 
 16442  the EOS application is still pending after 240 days have passed, the F-
 16443  1 student will no longer be authorized for employment and will need to 
 16444  stop engaging in on-campus employment. DHS is allowing a 240-day 
 16445  automatic extension period in order to minimize disruptions to on-
 16446  campus employment by teaching assistants, post-graduates working on 
 16447  research projects, and other positions that are integral to an F-1 
 16448  student's educational program. Note that the 240 days start after the 
 16449  expiration of one's current stay. DHS has always encouraged and will 
 16450  continue to encourage all nonimmigrants to apply for EOS within
 16451  
 16452  [[Page 45107]]
 16453  
 16454  the six months \328\ preceding the expiration of their current 
 16455  authorized stay thereby providing an additional buffer against any 
 16456  disruption of the ability to work.
 16457  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16458  
 16459      \327\ See 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)(i) for a description of on-campus 
 16460  employment. For on-campus employment that is based on severe 
 16461  economic hardship resulting from emergent circumstances pursuant to 
 16462  redesignated 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(vi), see later discussion for 
 16463  additional restrictions. The EOS application must be timely filed 
 16464  pursuant to the new paragraph at 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B). 
 16465  Moreover, if an F-1 student files an extension of stay application 
 16466  during the 30-day period provided in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v)(new), he 
 16467  or she does not receive an automatic extension of authorized 
 16468  employment, including on-campus, CPT, and severe economic hardship, 
 16469  and must wait for approval of the extension of stay application (and 
 16470  employment authorization application, if required) before engaging 
 16471  in CPT or employment. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii).
 16472      \328\ With respect to the earliest filing date for a Form I-539, 
 16473  there is no prohibition on filing the form before a certain date 
 16474  ahead of expiration.
 16475  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16476  
 16477      Likewise, DHS is allowing an automatic extension of off-campus 
 16478  employment authorization for up to 240-days during the pendency of the 
 16479  EOS application, for F-1 students who have demonstrated severe economic 
 16480  hardship pursuant to 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)(ii)(C) and previously received 
 16481  an EAD from USCIS that expired at the program end date that is now 
 16482  being extended with the EOS application. See new 8 CFR 
 16483  214.2(f)(5)(viii). These circumstances may include loss of financial 
 16484  aid or on-campus employment without fault on the part of the student, 
 16485  substantial fluctuations in the value of currency or exchange rate, 
 16486  inordinate increases in tuition and/or living costs, unexpected changes 
 16487  in the financial condition of the student's source of support, medical 
 16488  bills, or other substantial and unexpected expenses. In such cases, DHS 
 16489  believes a 240-day automatic extension of employment authorization will 
 16490  help alleviate the severe economic hardship and avoid a disruption in 
 16491  their employment, especially given the fact that an EAD is required and 
 16492  the frequency at which these students must submit an application for 
 16493  employment authorization.\329\ Additionally, given that USCIS's average 
 16494  EAD processing time is typically 60-120 days for foreign students and

 16496  flexibility in case of unexpected delays.
 16497  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 16498  
 16499      \329\ See 8 CFR 274a.12(c)(3). 8 CFR 214.2(f)(9)(ii)(F)(2) 
 16500  provides that employment authorization based upon severe economic 
 16501  hardship may be granted in one-year intervals up to the expected

 16725      DHS expects bona fide students to be committed to their studies, 
 16726  attending classes as required, carrying a full course of study, and 
 16727  making reasonable efforts toward program completion. Repeatedly failing 
 16728  classes demonstrates that the student is not making reasonable efforts 
 16729  toward completing his or her program of study. Therefore, a student who 
 16730  has a pattern of failing classes that has resulted in multiple program 
 16731  extensions would not be qualified for an EOS. The prohibition against 
 16732  requesting an EOS would not include students, such as those who, 
 16733  pursuant to DHS regulations, are making normal progress toward 
 16734  completing their program of study and still may not complete the 
 16735  program within 4 years
 16736  
 16737  [[Page 45109]]
 16738  
 16739  due to the standard timeline and requirements for the program. Absent

 16741  repeatedly failing classes, these students would be eligible for 
 16742  extension based upon compelling academic reasons. This prohibition also 
 16743  does not include cases where the DSO properly authorized the student to 
 16744  drop below a full course of study as well as cases in which the status 
 16745  has been reinstated following a loss of status. In such case, the 
 16746  student is eligible for reinstatement if the reduced course load was 
 16747  within the DSO's power to authorize. A student would be expected to 
 16748  provide evidence demonstrating the compelling academic reason in order 
 16749  for the DSO to recommend a program extension. The student may then 
 16750  apply for an EOS. While a letter from the student may be sufficient to 
 16751  meet his or her burden of proof, an immigration officer will evaluate 
 16752  the individual case and make the determination as to whether additional 
 16753  evidence (such as a letter from a member of the school administration 
 16754  or faculty) is needed to adjudicate the case.
 16755      DHS also proposed to clarify that a student can qualify for a 
 16756  program extension and corresponding EOS based on a documented illness 
 16757  or medical condition. To provide an objective standard, DHS proposed to 
 16758  codify standards already included in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(6)(iii)(B), which 
 16759  requires a student to provide medical documentation from a licensed 
 16760  medical doctor, licensed doctor of osteopathy, licensed psychologist, 
 16761  or licensed clinical psychologist to substantiate the illness or 
 16762  medical condition if seeking a reduced course load. See new 8 CFR 
 16763  214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(2). This is retained in the final rule. As this is 
 16764  already a long-standing requirement for DSOs and students in a similar 
 16765  context, DHS believes this will be appropriate and easy to implement in 
 16766  the program extension and corresponding EOS process. Further, requiring 
 16767  applicants to provide documentation of their medical illness or medical 
 16768  condition that caused their program delay is a reasonable request, 
 16769  because they are asking DHS to provide them additional time in the 
 16770  United States.
 16771      DHS also proposed a new factor in the EOS provisions--circumstances 
 16772  beyond the student's control, including a natural disaster, a national 
 16773  health crisis, or the closure of an institution. See new 8 CFR 
 16774  214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(2)(iii). This is retained in the final rule. As in 
 16775  the reinstatement context, DHS believes that there might be additional 
 16776  reasons beyond compelling academic or documented medical reasons that 
 16777  result in a student's inability to meet the program end date listed on 
 16778  the Form I-20.
 16779      Therefore, DHS proposed a third prong that encompasses scenarios 
 16780  that are not envisioned in the current provisions governing the 
 16781  extension of a program end date, such as those noted above. Some 
 16782  scenarios are currently in the reinstatement provisions, 8 CFR 
 16783  214.2(f)(16)(i)(F), such as natural disasters, pandemics, and the 
 16784  negligence of a DSO, and DHS believes that they merit favorable 
 16785  consideration in extension requests moving forward. Other scenarios may 
 16786  present circumstances that require a more intensive, fact-specific 
 16787  analysis and may fall into this proposed third prong. For example, the 
 16788  circumstances surrounding the closure of a school may be considered in 
 16789  determining whether the student qualifies for an EOS. By way of 
 16790  illustration, if a school closes as a result of a criminal conviction 
 16791  of its owners for engaging in student visa fraud by not requiring 
 16792  students to attend, but the student is unable to demonstrate that he or 
 16793  she was attending classes prior to closure as required to fulfill a 
 16794  full course of study, the closure of the institution might not qualify 
 16795  the student for a program extension. In contrast, if a school closes 
 16796  but a student is able to demonstrate that he or she was attending 
 16797  classes and was fulfilling all requirements to otherwise remain in 
 16798  status, the closure of the institute may qualify the student for a 
 16799  program extension.
 16800      The requirements to timely request an extension of the program end 
 16801  date would remain largely unchanged; however, DHS proposed a technical 
 16802  change to replace all references to the DSO ``granting'' an extension 
 16803  of the program with the term ``recommend'' an extension of the program 
 16804  in order for the student to file for EOS because USCIS, not the DSO, 
 16805  would ``grant'' the EOS. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(ii). This is 
 16806  retained in the final rule. For example, a student may not necessarily 
 16807  be granted an EOS by USCIS if an adjudicator determines the student has 
 16808  not actually maintained status or does not actually have compelling 
 16809  academic or documented medical reasons for the delay, despite the DSO's 
 16810  recommendation for program extension.
 16811      Where the alien requests a recommendation to extend the program end 
 16812  date, the DSO could only make a recommendation to extend the program if 
 16813  the alien requested the extension before the program end date noted on 
 16814  the most recent Form I-20, or successor form. Additionally, consistent 
 16815  with changes throughout this rule, once the DSO recommends the 
 16816  extension of the program, the alien would need to timely file for an 
 16817  EOS on the form and in the manner designated by USCIS, with the 
 16818  required fees and in accordance with the filing instructions, including

 16821  extraordinary circumstances. See 8 CFR 214.1(c)(4) and new 8 CFR 
 16822  214.2(f)(7)(ii) and (f)(7)(iii). This is retained in the final rule.
 16823      If seeking an EOS to engage in any type of practical training, the 
 16824  alien in F-1 status will also need to have a valid Form I-20, properly 
 16825  endorsed for practical training, and be eligible to receive the 
 16826  specific type of practical training requested. See new 8 CFR 
 16827  214.2(f)(7)(v). This is retained in the final rule. Finally, as with 
 16828  all immigration benefit requests, an immigration officer will generally 
 16829  not grant an EOS where an alien in F-1 status failed to maintain his or 
 16830  her status.
 16831      Finally, a student's failure to timely request, from the DSO, a 
 16832  recommendation for extension of the program end date prior to 
 16833  expiration of the student's authorized stay, which would result in the 
 16834  DSO recommending an extension of the program end date in SEVIS after 
 16835  the end date noted on the most recent Form I-20 or successor form, will

 16837  the alien will have failed to maintain status and will be ineligible

 16840  USCIS, with the required fee, including any biometrics required by 8 
 16841  CFR 103.16. DHS is also requiring F-2 dependents seeking to accompany

 16843  reinstatement, as applicable. These requirements are consistent with 
 16844  current provisions.

 16850  but would like the flexibility to use a new form if more efficient or 
 16851  responsive to workload needs. Thus, DHS is retaining its proposal to 
 16852  use general language to account for a possible change in form in

 16856  the future. See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A). If the form ever

  8560  student's program of study reflects upward academic progression. The 
  8561  list of educational levels that schools use to update their Form I-17, 
  8562  ``Petition for Approval of School for Attendance by Nonimmigrant 
  8563  student,'' is available at https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/sevis-help-hub/school-records/school-certification/form-i-17-listing-of-available-degrees. This list contains the following educational levels: 1. 
  8564  Primary and Secondary Education; 2. ELT; 3. Post-secondary 
  8565  Certificates/Non-Degree; 4. Associate; 5. Bachelor; 6. Master; 7. 
  8566  Doctorate. DHS may provide updated guidance on educational levels to 
  8567  ensure consistency across components and with ED.
  8568      DHS appreciates commenters' concerns about the rule's effect on 
  8569  academic growth of students. DHS recognizes academic pathways can be 
  8570  complex and that students may pursue multiple degrees or transition 
  8571  programs, including from undergraduate to graduate studies. The 
  8572  Department does not intend to discourage academic advancement or 
  8573  require students to abandon years of work.
  8574      DHS also recognizes the different approaches for undergraduate 
  8575  students and graduate students. This rule aims to balance program 
  8576  integrity and national security with the need to support legitimate 
  8577  educational pursuits. DHS believes differing approaches for 
  8578  undergraduate and graduate students are appropriate given the 
  8579  difference in the general ages of the students, a graduate student's 
  8580  previous opportunities to explore academic interests prior to entering 
  8581  graduate school, and a focus on more specific degree programs at the 
  8582  graduate level. DHS maintains it is appropriate to prohibit an F-1 
  8583  student at the graduate degree level or above from changing educational 
  8584  objectives at any point during their program of study for the reasons 
  8585  outlined above. However, DHS recognizes that extenuating circumstances, 
  8586  such as a school closure or a school's prolonged inability to hold in-
  8587  person classes due to a natural disaster, may prevent a graduate 
  8588  student from being able to continue their studies unless the student 
  8589  transfers to another SEVP-certified institution. The NPRM proposed 
  8590  prohibiting an F-1 student at the graduate level from transferring, 
  8591  without exception. DHS agrees with commenters that these situations may 
  8592  be outside the students' control and, taking this into consideration, 
  8593  DHS has amended the regulatory text to allow SEVP to authorize an 
  8594  exception to this transfer prohibition in extenuating circumstances. 
  8595  See new 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A), 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(i)(C), and 8 CFR 
  8596  214.2(f)(8)(i)(D). For the purposes of this rule, ``extenuating 
  8597  circumstances'' for a transfer are rare, exceptional events beyond the 
  8598  control of the school and the affected students that prevent an SEVP-
  8599  certified school from continuing to provide the student's approved 
  8600  course of study, such as a permanent or extended school closure, a 
  8601  school merger that eliminates the student's program, a loss of 
  8602  necessary authorization for the school to enroll F-1 students, or the 
  8603  school's prolonged inability to deliver required instruction due to a 
  8604  natural disaster or comparable emergency. In such circumstances, SEVP 
  8605  may, in its discretion and in coordination with the impacted SEVP-
  8606  certified school or schools, permit the transfer of student records to 
  8607  another SEVP-certified school so that the student may continue, to the 
  8608  extent practicable, in the same educational objective. This exception 
  8609  is narrow, is intended only to preserve continuity of study in 
  8610  emergency situations, does not create an entitlement to transfer, and 
  8611  does not otherwise authorize an F-1 student to change educational 
  8612  objectives. Affected students generally will access this exception 
  8613  through their DSOs, as SEVP becomes aware of qualifying extenuating 
  8614  circumstances through notifications from SEVP-certified schools and 
  8615  SEVP's existing outreach to schools during such events.
  8616      Regarding the claim that the rule will make Ph.D. enrollment 
  8617  riskier and result in unfilled teaching assistant and research 
  8618  positions, DHS does not intend for this rule to significantly affect 
  8619  these populations since foreign students may still study, teach, and 
  8620  research in the United States under this fixed period of admission 
  8621  framework. They may also apply for an EOS if they want to request an 
  8622  extension of their admission period and shouldn't experience any 
  8623  disruptions if they apply as early as possible (180 days) before the 
  8624  expiration of their current stay. Additionally, assistantships are 
  8625  awarded based on student need and should not be the primary motivation 
  8626  in enrolling foreign students.
  8627      Regarding comments on the relationship between graduate students 
  8628  and their faculty advisors and students choosing institutions based on 
  8629  faculty member's research, such students should consider applying for 
  8630  J-1 visas to better align their goals with the appropriate nonimmigrant 
  8631  status. DHS notes that J-1 categories include research scholars and 
  8632  college and university students, and requirements for transferring 
  8633  programs for J-1 students are governed by DoS regulations. See 22 CFR 
  8634  62.20, 62.23, 62.42.
  8635      DHS also acknowledges the request for simplified procedures for 
  8636  program extensions and transfers. DHS declines to alter the current 
  8637  procedures, as they are necessary for program integrity and national 
  8638  security. DHS will, however, evaluate needs for guidance to assist in 
  8639  the transition and application of these new rules and will provide this 
  8640  guidance to stakeholders as needed.
  8641      DHS recognizes commenters' request for clarification about what 
  8642  happens after the 240-days. The 240-day period offers certain F 
  8643  nonimmigrants the ability to continue with authorized employment for 
  8644  this time period while their EOS is pending. If the EOS takes longer 
  8645  than 240 days to adjudicate, the F nonimmigrant would need to stop 
  8646  authorized employment, but they can remain in the United States, can 
  8647  continue their full course of study, and are considered to be in a 
  8648  period of authorized stay during that period.
  8649  g. Delay and Suspension of Change in Educational Objectives
  8650      Comment: Commenters discussed several technical and implementation 
  8651  concerns regarding the proposed limitations on program changes and 
  8652  transfers. A commenter expressed concern that the discretionary 
  8653  provision in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E) may be exploited by future 
  8654  administrations. Other commenters opined DHS should not codify a 
  8655  regulation which cannot be implemented. Another commenter opined the 
  8656  delay or suspension of the educational objectives provision could 
  8657  create confusion and arbitrary outcomes. Similarly, a commenter thought 
  8658  8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E) would cause students, schools, and employers 
  8659  unnecessary uncertainty and resulting harm.
  8660      Response: DHS recognizes that this rule requires updates to SEVIS 
  8661  and other systems and it has been planning for these changes. The 
  8662  language proposed in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(E) would provide DHS 
  8663  authority to delay or suspend implementation of the provisions relating 
  8664  to a change in educational objectives, outlined in 8 CFR 
  8665  214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A) through (C), via announcement in the Federal 
  8666  Register and SEVP's website. DHS has given the comments on this 
  8667  provision considerable thought and agrees that this provision, as 
  8668  proposed, could cause unnecessary confusion and uncertainty
  8669

  8671  
  8672  in the future. DHS does not identify an indefinite need to suspend or 
  8673  delay the implementation of 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(A) through (C) and 
  8674  therefore, DHS has decided to amend 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(E) to limit the 
  8675  agencies' ability to delay or suspend implementation to two years from 
  8676  the effective date of this final rule.
  8677  2. Preparation for Departure
  8678  a. Support for Reducing the F-1 Departure Period From 60 to 30 Days
  8679      Comments: A few commenters expressed support to reduce the F-1 visa 
  8680  departure period from 60 days to 30 days. One commenter stated the 60-
  8681  day departure period was misaligned with enforcement objectives and 
  8682  increased the risk of visa overstays. This commenter referenced DHS 
  8683  reports showing above-average overstay rates in the student and 
  8684  exchange visitor visa categories. Another commenter stated that 
  8685  shortening the departure period would limit the risk of unauthorized 
  8686  employment or ``loitering'' after the lawful stay has ended.
  8687      Response: DHS appreciates the commenters' support for this rule and

  8689  strengthen oversight, and yield additional benefits to enhance the U.S. 
  8690  immigration system. This rule establishes an effective mechanism to 
  8691  periodically and directly assess whether nonimmigrants in F, J, and I 
  8692  status are complying with the conditions of their nonimmigrant 
  8693  classifications and U.S. immigration laws, and to obtain timely and 
  8694  accurate information about the activities these aliens have engaged in 
  8695  and plan to engage in during their temporary stay in the United States. 
  8696  DHS believes that this rule will encourage aliens to maintain lawful 
  8697  status and reduce instances in which aliens in F, J, and I nonimmigrant 
  8698  status unlawfully remain in the United States after their program, 
  8699  practical training, or activities or assignments end.
  8700  b. Opposition to Reducing the F-1 Departure Period From 60 to 30 Days

  8713  otherwise abuse the F-1 visas. Another commenter stated that the

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".

agency.description: Agency slugs, e.g. homeland-security-department, u-s-citizenship-and-immigration-services, u-s-immigration-and-customs-enforcement, state-department, labor-department, executive-office-of-the-president.
agency.title: Agency

pres_type.description: Presidential document subtypes (use with doc_type PRESDOCU).

cfr.description: CFR title:part affected, e.g. 8:214. The part must be numeric; lettered parts are not supported by this filter.
cfr.title: Cfr

tools.description: Search U.S. Federal Register documents (rules, proposed rules, notices, presidential documents) by keywords and filters. Prints document numbers, titles, types, dates, citations, dockets, RINs and abstracts.

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

(g) 2026-16231, Final Rule, Aug. 10, 2026, effective Sept. 9, 2026: requires the 9-11 Response and Biometric Entry-Exit Fee for covered H-1B/L-1 extension-of-status petitions even without a change of employer; in force and relevant to some post-graduation H-1B extensions.", "basis": "2026-17324, 91 FR 54817; C1-2026-17324, 91 FR 57516. 2026-18631, 91 FR 57807-57808, 57816. Proclamation 11069, 2026-19554, 91 FR 60497-60499 §§1-3. Executive Order 14431, 2026-19555, 91 FR 60501-60502 §§1-3. 2026-20660, 91 FR 64566. 2026-20955, 91 FR 65306-65310, amending 8 CFR 274a.13(d)-(e); STEM OPT non-change noted in 2026-14439, 91 FR 45002, 45037. 2026-16231, 91 FR 51360.", "uncertainty": "The proposed rules in (a), (b), and (e) could be finalized differently or not at all; no final versions were found through November 14, 2026."}, "Q11": {"answer": "The final rule does not set a new dollar filing fee in the regulatory text and does not guarantee a USCIS decision time. It repeatedly requires payment of the 'required'/'appropriate' fee as prescribed by the form and instructions, plus any required biometrics. Figures appearing in the preamble must be labelled carefully: a commenter referred to a $420 EOS filing fee and four EOS filings costing about $1,680; another commenter reported USCIS Service Center Operations taking more than 6.5 months to adjudicate 80 percent of EOS requests; another commenter reported California Service Center averages of 4.5 months for changes to F-1/J-1 and 3.5 months for extensions. Accurate handout draft: 'An extension of stay requires the USCIS fee and any biometrics required by the current Form I-539 instructions; the final rule does not set that fee amount in the regulation or guarantee a decision time. Commenter $420 figure: 2026-14439, 91 FR 45055; $1,680/four filings: 91 FR 45082. DHS response referring cost analysis to RIA Table 16 without adopting a regulatory fee: 91 FR 45082. Commenter processing figures: 91 FR 45063 (more than 6.5 months for 80 percent) and 91 FR 45082 (4.5/3.5 months). DHS no-guarantee statement: 91 FR 45025; six-month recommendation and no earliest-filing prohibition: 91 FR 45049 n.206, 45107 n.328, 45109-45110 & n.338.", "uncertainty": "Current Form I-539 instructions and any later USCIS fee schedule were outside the Federal Register documents reviewed; the handout should check the current instructions before printing a dollar amount."}, "Q12": {"answer": "(a) Most defensible answer: yes, for Priya's D/S-transition case, an I-539 received during the 60 days after her May 15, 2027 I-20 program end date—i.e., on or before July 14, 2027 (May 15 + 60 days)—should be treated as timely, because 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) specifically gives the transition group a period 'plus the departure period of 60 days,' and 214.1(m)(1)(i) describes filing 'before his or her period of admission expires, including the 60 day departure period.' There is nevertheless a textual tension: the general F-1 EOS rule, 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B), defines timely filing by reference to the new 30-day period in (f)(5)(v). An adviser should not wait for the 60 days without confirming current USCIS instructions. (b) No. Filing in the departure period does not preserve automatic on-campus or CPT employment. The rule states that if an EOS application is filed during the 30-day period in (f)(5)(v), the student 'does not receive an automatic extension of authorized employment, including on-campus, CPT, and severe economic hardship,' and (f)(7)(iii)(B) states that a student whose EOS is received during that 30-day period may continue a full course of study but 'may not continue or begin engaging in practical training or other employment.' For Priya, authorized employment under the transition provision in any event continues only until the program end date on the I-20 or EAD expiration. Recommendation: if uninterrupted on-campus/CPT work matters, USCIS should receive the I-539 before May 15, 2027 (the program end date), not during the post-program departure window; if she files after that date, she should stop employment until approval and any required employment authorization is granted.", "basis": "Transition 60-day period and OPT filing language: 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1), (m)(1)(i), as amended by 2026-14439, 91 FR 45123. General timely-filing/employment consequences: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B), 91 FR 45126; no automatic employment extension when filing in (f)(5)(v) period and 240-day cap otherwise: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(viii), 91 FR 45125-45126; preamble confirmation at 91 FR 45106-45107 & nn.327-328, 45109-45110.", "uncertainty": "The interaction between the transition-specific 60 days in 214.1(m)(1) and the general 30-day references in 214.2(f)(5)(v)/(f)(7)(iii)(B) is not expressly reconciled for non-OPT EOS filings; current Form I-539 instructions should be checked before advising reliance on days 31-60."}, "Q13": {"answer": "(a) After readmission on January 9, 2027, Sofia is no longer under the D/S transition period; CBP admits her under the fixed-date system. Her I-94 should run to the program end date on the I-20, May 14, 2027, plus the 30-day departure/status period in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v): May 14, 2027 + 30 days = June 13, 2027. She may remain without filing anything until June 13, 2027. (b) Yes. Q2.answer: (a) July 14, 2027. Provision: 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) (transition from D/S). Arithmetic: I-20 program end date May 15, 2027 + 60-day F departure period = July 14, 2027; this is earlier than the outer transition cap, so the cap does not change it. She has no EAD, so the 'later of EAD/program end' comparison uses May 15, 2027. (b) F: November 14, 2030. J: October 15, 2030. Arithmetic stated in the rule: September 15, 2026 + 4 years = September 15, 2030; + 60 days for F = November 14, 2030, and + 30 days for J = October 15, 2030. (c) Yes, as far as the five-month timing rule is concerned. She must begin classes at the new school within 5 months of transferring out or within 5 months of the program completion date on her current I-20, whichever is earlier. Program completion May 15, 2027 + 5 months = October 15, 2027; August 24, 2027 is before that date. This assumes the transfer-out/release mechanics are properly completed in SEVIS and she otherwise remains eligible. (d) Yes, on these facts she needs a USCIS filing for the new program unless she instead departs and is readmitted by CBP for the new program. Provisions supporting a USCIS extension-of-stay filing: 8 CFR 214.1(m)(1) (a D/S-transition student who 'would like to start a new program of study' must apply for an EOS with USCIS); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(D) (a student seeking a change in educational objectives must, if seeking an EOS, apply on the USCIS form with fee/biometrics); 8 CFR 214.2(f)(8)(iv) (if the new program will not be completed within the authorized period in (f)(5)(i), the student must apply to USCIS for an EOS with a valid endorsed I-20 showing the new program end date); and 8 CFR 214.1(c)(2) (a nonimmigrant seeking to stay beyond the currently authorized period must file the prescribed EOS form with fees/evidence/biometrics). Her transition authorization ends July 14, 2027, before the August 24, 2027 master's start, so the new program is outside the period already authorized. (e) She does not need a Form I-539 for the OPT period if she remains within the transition exemption; she files only the Form I-765 on these facts. She is recommended for post-completion OPT, files the I-765 on March 1, 2027 (on or before March 18, 2027), and files before her transition admission period (including the 60-day departure period) expires. If OPT is approved as requested through June 13, 2028, she may remain until that EAD expiration + 60 days = August 12, 2028 (June 13, 2028 + 60 days).

For (d), departure/readmission is an alternative route recognized elsewhere in the rule, but CBP admission is discretionary.

Q3.answer: (a) December 13, 2026. Arithmetic: program start/report date January 12, 2027 minus 30 days = December 13, 2026. He actually entered December 20, 2026, which is within that window. (b) January 17, 2028. Arithmetic: I-20 program end December 18, 2027 + 30-day period in 8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(v) reflected on the I-94 = January 17, 2028. (c) Yes. Provision: 8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(2)(i) (compelling academic reason), which expressly lists 'unexpected change in faculty advisor' as an example of an unexpected research problem. A reason the rule says is not acceptable: delays caused by academic probation or suspension, or by a student's repeated inability or unwillingness to complete the course of study; (f)(7)(i)(C)(2)(i) states these are 'not acceptable reasons.' (d) The DSO recommendation must be requested/entered before the program end date on the most recent I-20 passes; after that end date has passed, the student is no longer on the EOS track. Consequence if missed: if the DSO enters an extension of the program end date in SEVIS after the end date on the most recent I-20 has passed, the student must file for reinstatement of F-1 status (with fee/biometrics), and dependents must file EOS or reinstatement as applicable. (e) To keep the RA job without interruption, USCIS must receive the I-539 no later than December 18, 2027 (the program end date, i.e., before the 30-day (f)(5)(v) period begins). A later filing can still be timely for EOS/study if USCIS receives it on or before January 17, 2028 (the I-94 date including the 30-day period), but then he may not continue or begin employment/practical training while it is pending and must wait for approval (and any required EAD) before resuming. (f) If filed in time to preserve employment, the on-campus employment is automatically extended during pendency for up to 240 days beginning from the I-94 end date. Approximate end: January 17, 2028 + 240 days = approximately September 13, 2028 (2028 is a leap year); work must stop after that if USCIS has not approved, although he may remain and study until USCIS decides. (g) If approved for the new I-20 end date, the authorized stay should run to May 19, 2028 + 30 days = June 18, 2028. If denied after the I-94 date has passed, he and any dependents must immediately depart the United States.

The issued receipt/approval notices and I-9 documentation should be checked.

Q4.answer: (a) The trip does not automatically put the pending I-539 at risk if, at re-entry, he seeks admission only for the balance of the previously authorized period and that period has not expired. His previously authorized period runs to January 17, 2028, so a January 5, 2028 return is before expiration. How he presents himself matters: if he instead seeks admission with an I-20 for a program end date beyond the previously authorized period (the May 19, 2028 I-20) while the EOS is pending, USCIS may deem the EOS abandoned and CBP's new admission, if granted, will govern. He should carry a copy of the Form I-797C receipt for the I-539 (or I-765) together with the proposed length of stay as evidenced by the I-20/DS-2019 or employment letter. (b) For a different student with a pending application to change from F-1 to another nonimmigrant status, departure while the change-of-status application is pending causes USCIS to consider the change-of-status application abandoned.
Q4.basis: (a) Non-abandonment for balance-of-prior-period re-entry: 8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(i), as amended by 2026-14439, 91 FR 45123; possible abandonment when seeking admission on an I-20/DS-2019 beyond the prior authorized period: 8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(ii), 91 FR 45123; admission categories for pending/approved EOS: 8 CFR 214.1(a)(4)(i)(B)-(C), 91 FR 45122; travel document instruction: 8 CFR 214.1(c)(8)(iii), 91 FR 45123; preamble scenarios at 91 FR 45098-45099. (b) Abandonment of change-of-status application: new 8 CFR 248.1(f), 91 FR 45130-45131.
